IB 2027 · SL · Unit 5

Unit 5: The OOP Paradigm

SL curriculum overview and structured learning plan.

Introduction

How do classes and objects help you build software that scales?

This unit introduces object-oriented programming as a way to organize code around objects that combine data and behavior. You will move from writing isolated procedures to designing reusable classes with clear responsibilities.

You will evaluate the strengths and limits of OOP, design class structures with UML, distinguish static and instance members, construct class code with __init__ and self, and apply encapsulation to protect data integrity.

Why OOP is used

OOP helps large programs stay manageable by splitting responsibility across classes.

  • Modularity: each class has a focused role.
  • Reusability: once a class is written, it can be used in other projects.
  • Encapsulation: class data is updated through controlled methods.
Class design with UML

Before coding, you design classes using UML class diagrams.

  • Top row: class name
  • Middle row: attributes and data types
  • Bottom row: methods and signatures
  • + public, - private visibility
Static vs instance members

Some values belong to every object; others belong to one specific object.

  • Instance: unique per object, e.g. self.balance.
  • Static: shared by all objects, e.g. next_id.
Constructing safe classes

You will construct class code and protect data through encapsulation.

  • Define classes with constructors (__init__).
  • Create objects through instantiation.
  • Use getters/setters to validate updates.
Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Class A blueprint that defines attributes and methods for a type of object.
Object (Instance) A concrete item created from a class at runtime.
Constructor (__init__) A method that runs during object creation to initialize state.
Attribute Data stored in an object or class.
Method A function that belongs to a class.
UML Class Diagram A three-row diagram showing class name, attributes, and methods.
Static Variable Data shared by all instances of a class.
Instance Variable Data unique to one specific object.
Encapsulation Protecting internal data by exposing controlled methods for access and updates.
Accessor / Mutator Getter and setter methods used to read and validate updates to internal state.

Syllabus Coverage

  • B3.1.1 OOP fundamentals
  • B3.1.2 Class design (UML)
  • B3.1.3 Static vs non-static members
  • B3.1.4 Class definition and instantiation
  • B3.1.5 Encapsulation and information hiding

Applications

  • Bank account and transaction systems
  • School information and enrollment systems
  • Inventory and stock management
  • Game entities (player, item, enemy)
  • Reusable UI component libraries
